migrationNotes: Spine: take one promise and test it against everything that can happen, finding the single case that breaks it, then meet the same four cases in a table.
Each stop adds one case: pass and lunch, pass and no lunch, then the two failed-test days; the table at the end puts all four side by side.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): if-then-claims-hook, if-then-claims-silent.

lesson.title: If-then claims

steps.headline: The two halves of a promise

lead.text: Look at Sam's sentence again: “If you pass your test, I'll buy you lunch.” It has two halves joined by “if … then”. A sentence of that shape is called a conditional, because what Sam does depends on something else happening first.

The half after “if” is the antecedent: you pass your test. The half after “then” is the consequent: Sam buys you lunch. The antecedent sets the condition, and the consequent says what follows when the condition is met.

Each half is a claim in its own right, so each can be true or false. That lets us use the short names from the last lesson. Call the antecedent p and the consequent q, and write the whole sentence as p → q, with the arrow reading “if … then”. The order matters. In p → q the condition always comes first, and the rest of the lesson depends on telling the two halves apart.

diagram.alt: Sam's promise split into two boxes joined by an arrow. The left box is the antecedent, you pass your test, called p. The right box is the consequent, Sam buys you lunch, called q.
diagram.caption: Sam's promise as p → q. The condition comes first and the arrow points to what follows.

steps.headline: When a promise can be broken

lead.text: A promise can only be broken in a situation it covers. Sam's covers the situation where you pass, and in that situation there are two possibilities. You pass and Sam buys the lunch, so he has kept his word. You pass and Sam doesn't buy the lunch, so he has broken it.

Notice what the broken case needs. The condition has been met, because you passed, and the result is missing, because there was no lunch. A condition that is met is what puts the promise to the test, and a missing result is what fails the test.
That covers the days when you pass. It leaves the days when you fail the test, and the promise has to be read carefully there. The next few screens take it case by case.

diagram.alt: Two outcomes on a day you pass the test. Sam buys lunch and the promise is kept, or Sam buys no lunch and the promise is broken.
diagram.caption: You pass in both pictures. Only the lunch differs, and only one of them breaks the promise.

lead.text: Let p mean “The access code is correct” and q mean “The door opens.” The rule p → q is a promise from the door.

reveal.text: Compare your choice with the one case where the code is right and the door stays shut. That is Sam's pass-and-no-lunch again, with a door in place of Sam.

lead.text: Now the days the promise doesn't cover. You fail the test, and Sam buys lunch anyway. He promised lunch if you passed, and you didn't pass, so the condition was never met. Whatever Sam does now, he hasn't gone against what he said. Buying you lunch is a generous extra, and it contradicts nothing.

The same goes for the day when you fail and Sam buys no lunch. He said nothing about that day either, and nobody can accuse him of breaking a promise that didn't apply. On both days the promise is untouched. In logic we call the conditional true in those cases, meaning that it has not been broken.

That is a convention, and it helps to state it plainly. A conditional gets the value false when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false. When the antecedent is false, the conditional is true whatever the consequent does.

diagram.alt: Two outcomes on a day you fail the test. Sam buys lunch anyway, or buys none. In both the promise is untouched.
diagram.caption: The condition is false in both pictures, so the promise was never put to the test.

lead.text: Use the access-code rule again, with p for “The code is correct” and q for “The door opens.” This time the code is wrong and the door stays shut.
p and q can each be true or false, which makes four cases in all. You have now decided what the rule says in every one of them.

Here are the four cases side by side. Each row says whether p and q are true, and the last column says whether p → q is true in that row. A list of every case with the result beside each is how logicians check anything that depends on a few claims, and the course uses it a lot.

afterFigure.text: Read the table with Sam in mind. Only the second row is false, and it is the pass-and-no-lunch row. The other three are true, and two of them are rows where the condition was never met. A false antecedent hands you a true conditional automatically.

One mistake to watch for is reading a true consequent as a sign that the antecedent was true. In the third row q is true and p is false. A lunch bought on a day you failed says nothing about whether you passed.

lead.text: Take the rule “If a shape is a square, it has four sides.” A rectangle with four sides turns up. It isn't a square.

lesson.orientation: State exactly when a conditional is false, and resist the pull to read it as a promise about the antecedent.
lesson.nextAction: Recognise that a conditional and its contrapositive say the same thing, while its converse does not.

blocks.text: Sam says to you: “If you pass your test, I'll buy you lunch.” The test comes and you fail. A week later Sam turns up and buys you lunch anyway.

It is tempting to say that something odd has happened, as if the promise had been quietly swapped for a different one. People disagree about this. Some say Sam broke his promise by giving you something you hadn't earned. Others say he kept it. Settling it means finding out exactly what the promise covers.

Sentences built with “if … then” turn up in rules, in laws and in the small print of every prize draw, and a mistake in reading them is easy to make. This lesson takes Sam's promise apart and lists everything that can happen to it. One situation turns out to break it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the one case that breaks an if-then rule, and see why a failed condition never breaks it.

recap.keyIdea: A conditional p → q is false in exactly one case: p true and q false. Every other case leaves it true.

blocks.text: Back to Sam: failing the test and getting lunch anyway breaks nothing, because the promise only covers the case where you pass. You found the one case that breaks the door's rule, and you showed that a four-sided rectangle that isn't a square leaves “If it's a square, it has four sides” untouched.

recap.nextHook: Sam's promise runs from passing to lunch. The next lesson turns a rule round to see whether the version that runs the other way says the same thing.

questions.prompt: Which case makes p → q false?
hints: A promise is broken when what was promised does not happen.
Find the case where the code is right but the door stays shut.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The code is correct but the door stays shut: p true, q false.

questions.onCorrect: p true, q false: the code is right and the door stays shut. That is the one case where the promise fails.

misconceptions.feedback: Here the code is wrong, so the door has made no promise to break.
Here the code is wrong too. The door only promised something about correct codes.

questions.prompt: How many of the four cases make p → q true?
hints: List the four cases: p and q each true or false.
Which one case breaks the promise?
Count the cases that are left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the true–false case is false, so three cases are true.

questions.onCorrect: Three. Only one case breaks the promise, so the other three leave it true.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of false cases. The question asks for the true ones.
One case does break a promise. Find it and take it away.
Count the cases where p is false as well as those where p is true. Only one case breaks the promise.

questions.prompt: When p and q are both false, is p → q true or false?
hints: With a wrong code, was the door's promise put to the test?
Does this case break the rule?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A false antecedent makes the conditional true.

questions.onCorrect: True. With p false the rule isn't tested, so nothing breaks it.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule only promised something about correct codes. Does this case break that?

questions.prompt: Let p mean “The shape is a square” and q mean “The shape has four sides.” Is p → q true or false for a four-sided rectangle that is not a square?
hints: Is p true or false for this shape?
Is this the case where p is true and q is false?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: p is false for this rectangle, so the rule is not broken: p → q is true.

questions.onCorrect: True. The shape isn't a square, so the rule about squares is untouched. A true q doesn't make p true.

misconceptions.feedback: p is false for this shape. A rule about squares can't be broken by a shape that isn't one.

questions.prompt: p is true and q is false. Is p → q true or false?
hints: Check the case where the antecedent holds but the consequent doesn't.
That case is the one the conditional rules out.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its antecedent holds and its consequent fails.

questions.onCorrect: False. The antecedent holds and the consequent fails: the one case that breaks a conditional.

misconceptions.feedback: p holds, so the conditional is being tested. Does q deliver what p promised?

questions.prompt: How many of the four cases make a conditional false?
hints: Go through each combination of p and q.
A false conditional needs p to hold and q to fail.
How many combinations meet both conditions?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Exactly one case is false: true antecedent, false consequent.

questions.onCorrect: One: p true and q false. Every other combination leaves the conditional true.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many cases are true. Count the false ones.
A false conditional needs p true and q false together. How many combinations do that?
A broken promise is possible. Find the combination that breaks it.

questions.prompt: Did Sam break his promise? Answer yes or no.
hints: Who was the promise about: people who passed, or people who failed?
What would Sam have to do to be caught out?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. The promise only covered the case where you passed.

questions.onCorrect: No. Sam only promised something about passing. A kind act in another case can't break it.

misconceptions.feedback: Look at what the promise covers. Is it about people who failed?

questions.prompt: In “If the code is correct, the door opens”, which part is the antecedent?
hints: The antecedent is the part after “if”.
The consequent is the part after “then”.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The antecedent follows “if”: the code is correct.

questions.onCorrect: The part after “if” is the antecedent. The part after “then” is the consequent.

misconceptions.feedback: That part comes after “then”. It is the consequent, not the antecedent.
The antecedent is one part of the sentence, the part that sets the condition.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't the match being cancelled without rain break the promise?
hints: Read the promise again. Which days does it cover?

acceptedIdeas: The promise only speaks about rainy days.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The promise only speaks about rainy days, so a dry day can't break it.

questions.onCorrect: The promise covers only rainy days. On a dry day it says nothing, so it can't be broken.

choices.label: The promise only speaks about rainy days.
A cancelled match always keeps a promise.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule doesn't say rain is the only cause, or even a cause. It says what follows when it rains.
A cancelled match keeps this promise only on a rainy day. Dry days are not covered at all.

questions.prompt: The rule is “If a number is divisible by 4, it is even.” Which number would break it?
hints: A rule breaks only when its first part holds and its second part fails.
Test each number against both parts of the rule.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: None of them. To break the rule a number would have to be divisible by 4 and odd.

questions.onCorrect: None. Breaking the rule needs a multiple of 4 that is odd, and 8 is divisible by 4 and even.

misconceptions.feedback: 6 isn't divisible by 4, so the rule says nothing about it.
7 isn't divisible by 4, so the rule has no say about it.
8 is divisible by 4. Is it also even?
